Everything you type here saves by itself. There is no save button and you cannot lose your work. Close the page whenever you like and come back.

📋 What to do

  1. You do not have to get through all of them. Armin decided this on 13 August, right after you said the dashboard was overwhelming because of how many videos there were to watch. His words: “you don’t have to review all of them if it’s overwhelming. Just review as many as you can.” That still stands. Start at the top, stop when you want to stop, and nothing below where you stopped is owed by you.
  2. If you are using everything on a clip, press one button. Use everything on this clip answers all seven questions at once - the video, all three covers, all three titles. Most clips should be one press and nothing else.
  3. The video first. Press Watch, then answer Am I using this video?
    • Not using it means the whole clip is out - the covers and the titles go with it, and you do not have to answer anything else on that clip. Just write one line saying why, so the next batch is better.
    • Using it opens the covers and the titles below.
  4. Each cover, one at a time: are you using it? You are not picking one winner. Three covers always go up and YouTube tests them against each other, so whatever you do not take from us, you make yourself:
    • Using all 3 of ours - you make none.
    • Using 2 of ours - you make 1 of your own, and the three compete.
    • Using 1 of ours - you make 2 of your own.
    • Using none of ours - you make all 3 yourself.
    The page does this arithmetic for you and says it under each clip, so you can always see what you have told us.
  5. Each title, the same way, and separately from its cover. A cover can be good under a title that is wrong, and a title can be right over a cover you do not like - so they are two answers, not one. Ask: does the video actually say the thing this title says?
    • Title says secret, hidden, or behind their back - did anyone actually say it was secret? If not, do not use it.
    • Title says something big like civil war, coup, or invasion - did they actually say those words?
    • Title names a place or a person, like Europe or Trump - is the video really about them?
    • Is the title about the main thing in the video, or a small part near the end? It should be the main thing.
    You never have to write a better one. Press Not using it and, if you can, say in a few words what was wrong. Titles work the same as covers: whatever you do not take, you write yourself.
  6. Tap any cover to see it full size. To save one, press Save this cover - if your browser does not start the download, right-click that same button and choose Save link as. Either way the file is already named after the video's title, so you never have to rename it. Copy title gives you the matching title text.
  7. If a clip has a Subtitles box, upload that file too. Right-click Save subtitles, choose Save link as, then on YouTube go to Subtitles, ADD LANGUAGE, English, Upload file, With timing. It takes about 20 seconds and it is worth it: our subtitles spell the Iranian names correctly and YouTube's automatic ones do not, and those names are what people search for. Not every clip will have one - only the longer ones to start with.
  8. When you have gone through them all, press Submit all feedback at the bottom. It gives you one block of text - send that to Armin. One message for everything, not one per clip.

Blunt is more useful than polite. When you do not use something, one line about why is worth more to us than anything else on this page - it is the only way the next batch gets better. "Bad" on its own does not tell us what to change.

A clip you have not answered is not the same as a clip you approved. Anything you leave blank is reported as not answered, so nothing gets published on the assumption that your silence meant yes.

Each stream below has its own coloured dot, and the feedback button under it carries the same dot, so you can always tell which stream a button belongs to.

A five day plan to end the Islamic Republic, costed at about five billion dollars and no ground invasion. Jeff lays out the case in full. He starts with why American carriers are stretched thin at all, tracing it back through the Clinton era cuts from a two major theatre posture to one, the twenty years the war on terror consumed, and the rebuilding that has been started and interrupted twice since. His conclusion is blunt: you fight with the military you have, not the one you wish you had, which is why crews are being rotated now rather than reinforced. Then the plan itself. Strike the regime with non-critical munitions, obliterate it as a functioning state inside 120 hours, and give a mass uprising the best chance it will ever get. The operation runs a little under two billion dollars, five billion all in, against a war that would otherwise be paid for in Iranian blood over years. He also makes the case for where American force is going next: autonomous strike, cheap long range munitions, machine vision that lets a missile pick its own target without any outside feed. Exaggerating what the Islamic Republic does is not harmless. It hands the regime a way to discredit everything else you say. A caller tells Armin her favourite thing he has ever said on stream is that it is not true the regime automatically arrests or executes every woman who shows her hair. Not because the regime deserves the correction, but because the exaggeration is a weapon that gets used against the people making it. Armin's argument is that this is a choice between wanting to defeat your enemy and wanting to demonise them, and that only one of those actually wins. If you deny something your opponent genuinely did, the first person who produces the evidence has proved you are unreliable, and every true accusation you have ever made goes down with it. He makes the point with a deliberately extreme analogy about propaganda photographs, and lands on the practical rule: when a regime has committed real atrocities, you already have more than enough to work with. Inventing more is a losing trade. The subsidies are now ending because the war has cut the revenue that paid for them, and the regime believes the cut is what will trigger an uprising. So it has three strategies, and Armin walks through each. Announce an unbearable price first, then a smaller one, so the smaller one feels like relief. Description

CNN has reported a morale and supply crisis aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln after more than 250 consecutive days at sea, and the sourcing is the part nobody is examining. Armin walks through what the report actually rests on: not interviews with sailors, but one person relaying what family members say they were told, which puts several degrees of separation between the claim and anyone who has been on the ship. A caller who has served explains what life on a carrier is actually like, from swim breaks with sharpshooters watching for sharks to a supply ship that restocks food and fuel alongside ammunition, and argues the food shortage claim does not survive contact with how the Navy operates. What is conceded openly is that some sailors on a 250-day deployment are under real mental pressure, that this is what war is, and that a US defence official has confirmed one sailor went overboard in July. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has called the wider picture exaggerated. Armin's argument is about who benefits: whatever the truth of the individual cases, a mainstream American outlet saying the superpower's sailors are breaking is the single most useful piece of footage the Islamic Republic could be handed, and it will run on Iranian state television as proof the regime has humiliated the United States. ðŸ”´ Live every day: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCAbKpmZxZBs4eMtgE1Da8bQ/streams Join our daily group calls: https://www.skool.com/libertypolitics/about Join our daily group calls: https://www.skool.com/libertypolitics/about

Description

Armin reads a Charlie Kirk post arguing that hate speech does not exist legally in America, and then makes the consequentialist case for free speech rather than the sentimental one. We do not defend free speech because it feels good to defend, he says, but because freer societies are demonstrably more prosperous, stronger and better, and the comparison he reaches for is the United Kingdom against the United States. Pushing back against bad ideas is the job of citizens; the government's job is to make it safe for them to do it. Reaching for the state every time something ugly is said is lazy, and it creates a bigger problem than the one being solved. Hand a government the power to decide which ideas are acceptable and you have built a truth ministry and a morality police. It may even get it right this time, but your own views will be reclassified eventually, and the power ends up being used to keep the government in place rather than to keep bad ideas out. He also argues Islam grows fastest in darkness, which is why he wants extremists visible rather than underground. Roy pushes back hard on where the line falls between targeting ideas and targeting people, and Armin answers with the American standard: direct threats of harm against individuals are illegal, and everything short of that stays legal. ✏️ This title C
Save this cover
Description

A Burger King worker was fired after saying Free Palestine to a customer, started a fundraiser, and passed 229,000 dollars. Armin uses the story to draw the distinction almost everyone gets wrong. Being fired is not a violation of your free speech. It is your employer exercising theirs. Free speech protects you from the government: from imprisonment, from fines, from torture, from the death penalty, and from the state withdrawing its protection because of something you said. It does not protect you from other people responding, from being deplatformed by a private company, or from losing a job. He is also clear that the fundraiser is a symptom rather than the disease. The money is a measure of how far American attitudes on Israel and Palestine have moved, and that shift is the actual problem, not the total on the page. His view on silencing people is unchanged: it reliably backfires, and it turns whoever was silenced into a star.
